title: West Indies' Plan B Against Abhishek Sharma Revealed — and It Failed
excerpt: Shamar Springer admitted the visitors shelved their attacking playbook and tried to starve Abhishek of boundaries. Abhishek knew exactly what was coming — and dismantled it anyway.
body:
• West Indies all-rounder Shamar Springer revealed the team's "Plan B" after the third T20I in Indore: stop trying to dismiss Abhishek Sharma and bowl defensively to limit him to singles and twos.
  • Abhishek knew exactly what was coming. Roston Chase had dismissed him in the first two T20Is, so he played Chase's opening over cautiously — then attacked him through the off side.
  • The tactic failed completely: Abhishek smashed 69 off 30 balls and became the fastest batter to 2,000 T20I runs (1,024 balls, 140 fewer than Suryakumar Yadav's 1,164).
  • India posted 223 and won by 14 runs (West Indies 209 for 7) to take a 2-1 series lead — the first time on this tour a team successfully defended a total.

The admission

West Indies did not lose the third T20I in Indore for lack of a plan. They lost it because their plan met Abhishek Sharma. After India's 14-run victory on October 11 — India 223, West Indies 209 for 7 — all-rounder Shamar Springer told the press conference that the visitors had deliberately shelved their attacking instincts against India's opener and fallen back on damage control.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2109350029098107069

"Our Plan B was to just be as defensive as possible and try to make him get singles and twos rather than boundaries. Nothing too extravagant."

— Shamar Springer, West Indies all-rounder

"There is not really much you could do besides be defensive," Springer added. "The wickets are so good and those players are world-class players. They are the best for a reason."

Context & Background

The tactical battle had been building all series. Roston Chase's offspin had dismissed Abhishek in both the first and second T20Is, and when West Indies won the toss and bowled first in Indore — captain Shai Hope's explanation was blunt, "for obvious reasons" — Chase opened the bowling. Chasing sides had won every match on the tour so far, mocking up targets as large as 406 in the third ODI and 250 in the second T20I, and the short Holkar Stadium boundaries (63 metres square, 72 straight) promised another shootout.

So Abhishek did something unusual for a batter with a 194.94 career strike rate: he blocked. For the first 2.2 overs he collected only singles, reaching 5 off 6 balls. He had seen the trap coming.

"I knew they had a plan against me — the offspinner bowling the first over."

— Abhishek Sharma, after the match

Impact & Analysis

Once the respect period ended, Abhishek turned the plan inside out. Off the third ball of the third over he stepped away and smashed Chase through the covers for his first boundary. When Chase slowed one to 86.9kph to buy his wicket, Abhishek made room and launched it over wide long-off for six — then repeated the dose over the covers. In four deliveries his strike rate leapt from 100 to 233.33. Captain Hope was forced to take Chase off despite two left-handers at the crease.

Springer replaced him and conceded 4, 4, 6 off successive deliveries. The seamers switched to yorkers, straight and wide, but kept missing their lengths; Abhishek kept slicing them through the arc between cover and point — the best of them a full-toss yorker from Shamar Joseph that he took on the full and steered through a gap at point, leaving Joseph with a wry smile.

The numbers underline the dominance: 50 of his 69 runs came through the off side — 72.5%, the highest share of off-side runs in any of his T20I innings of 50 or more. His fifty arrived off 18 balls, inside the powerplay, and the 2,000-run milestone fell in just 1,024 balls. Chase returned later to dismiss Ishan Kishan and Shreyas Iyer in the same over — a reminder, as ESPNcricinfo's tactical breakdown noted, of how much Abhishek's initial assault had mattered.

For West Indies, the deeper worry is strategic, not technical. Containment as a Plan B worked only until Abhishek decided to end it — and Springer himself admitted the pitch (lower than expected, no dew arriving despite their gamble) meant their bowlers executed worse than India's. When your fallback plan against one batter fails this publicly, the remaining two games demand a new idea.

What's Next

India lead the five-match series 2-1 with two games to play. West Indies must now find a third way: their attacking plan (Chase's offspin) worked twice, their defensive plan (Springer's Plan B) worked for barely four overs. For India, the concern is thinner — the middle order was quiet and the chase came closer than 223 should have allowed — but as long as Abhishek is reading their opponents' plans before the first over is bowled, Shreyas Iyer's side hold the edge. Springer's full post-match comments make clear West Indies know it.
